questions.q: Identify the narrator of "How I Taught My Grandmother to Read" and quote the first sentence that confirms the first-person perspective.
questions.a: The narrator is the granddaughter (Sudha Murty as a young girl). The opening line "I was very happy when my grandmother decided to learn to read" uses "I" and "my," establishing first-person perspective. A wrong answer naming "the grandmother" or "an outside narrator" reveals the student cannot distinguish between the protagonist (Krishtakka) and the narrator, a fundamental confusion between character and narrative voice.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the granddaughter's statement "I never saw my grandmother cry" is significant given the first-person perspective.
questions.a: The statement reveals the narrator's limited knowledge — she only knows what she personally witnessed. Since the narration is first-person, the reader also cannot know if Krishtakka cried privately. A wrong answer saying "the grandmother never cried" treats the narrator's limited observation as absolute fact, missing that first-person narration restricts access to other characters' inner lives and off-screen actions.

questions.q: The narrator describes her grandmother as "old and illiterate" early in the story. Later, Krishtakka touches the narrator's feet as a mark of respect. Using first-person perspective analysis, explain how the narrator's description of this moment reveals her changing perception.
questions.a: Step 1: Locate the scene where Krishtakka touches the narrator's feet (after learning to read). Step 2: Note the narrator's reaction — surprise, humility, described through her internal thoughts ("I felt small"). Step 3: Recognize that first-person narration lets us experience this shift in real-time — we feel the narrator's realization that her "old, illiterate" grandmother possesses wisdom and dignity. Step 4: Conclude that the perspective forces readers to undergo the same reassessment. A wrong answer merely summarizing the event without analyzing the perspective's role misses the analytical requirement.

questions.q: Compare how the story would differ if told from Krishtakka's first-person perspective versus the granddaughter's. Identify two specific scenes that would change significantly.
questions.a: From Krishtakka's perspective: (1) The opening — we'd hear her internal motivation for learning (dependence on others to read *Kashi Yatre*), not the granddaughter's amusement. (2) The climax — the moment of reading the novel herself would be an internal triumph, not an observed event. The granddaughter's perspective creates dramatic irony (we see Krishtakka's determination before the narrator fully appreciates it); Krishtakka's perspective would create intimate access to her struggle but lose the intergenerational discovery dynamic. A wrong answer listing plot points without analyzing perspective shift shows inability to isolate narrative technique from story content.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The first-person narration in this story makes the theme of empowerment less effective because we only see the grandmother through the granddaughter's eyes." Defend or refute with evidence.
questions.a: Refute. The limited perspective *strengthens* the empowerment theme. Because we see Krishtakka initially through the narrator's condescending lens ("old," "illiterate," "dependent"), her transformation into an independent reader who touches her teacher's feet carries greater emotional weight. The narrator's own growth — from amusement to reverence — mirrors the reader's journey. First-person narration makes empowerment a *shared discovery*, not a reported fact. A wrong answer agreeing with the claim confuses "limited perspective" with "weak portrayal," missing how narrative irony serves thematic depth.

questions.q: Write a 4-sentence paragraph from the perspective of the *Kashi Yatre* novel itself, watching Krishtakka learn to read. Use first-person narration ("I") and include one metaphor.
questions.a: I waited patiently on the shelf, a silent witness to her fingers tracing my spine like a blind woman reading Braille. Each week her touch grew surer, her lips moving less, her eyes owning my words. When she finally read me aloud to her granddaughter, I felt my pages turn to wings. I was no longer a book — I had become her bridge to the world. A poor answer writes in third person, omits the metaphor, or describes the plot without adopting the novel's voice, showing inability to manipulate perspective creatively.
